messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thong Nguyen was sixty-eight years old when he finally sat in a therapist’s office, five years after his wife Lan was killed in the carjacking. They had just parked in their own driveway when a young man appeared at Lan’s window. Thong saw the gun, heard the single shot, and then watched his wife slump forward. In the weeks and months that followed, the memory never came as a whole story; it arrived in shards—the glint of the barrel, the sound of the bullet, the weight of her body as he tried to pull her upright. When these fragments surfaced, he often heard the gunshot ringing in his head, and a grief so vast it would press him into his chair until his daughter called his name. He had come to believe that if he had switched seats with her, she would still be alive.

Those memory fragments did not stay in the past. They made him feel that danger was still right there, even in his own living room. He began checking the front door lock three, four, sometimes a dozen times before he could settle into a chair. His heart would hammer at a car backfiring or a neighbor’s knock—false alarms that left him trembling with fear and a gnawing shame. The more the fragmented memories broke through, the more convinced he became that dangerous people were everywhere, and that he had to stay ready. At the courthouse, where he had worked as a public defender for forty years, he now scanned every visitor’s face for hidden threat, avoiding eye contact with men who wore hoodies or kept their hands in their pockets.

Feeling this constantly on edge exhausted him, and Thong had developed his own ways of coping. He would stop at a fast‑food place on the way home and eat an extra burger and fries, not because he was hungry but because the chewing and tasting blunted the sharp edges of the day. He stopped watching the evening news; crime dramas and even courtroom movies were out of the question because they could trigger a memory fragment that would leave him staring at the wall. Yet these strategies sometimes backfired. When he overate and then felt sluggish, he would become even more vigilant, convinced that his dulled attention made him an easy target. And when he avoided a television show, he would later find himself hypervigilant in a quiet room, jumping at the creak of a floorboard—a false alarm that dragged the memory of the gunshot back into his mind with full force.

His hypervigilance toward people often created a self‑reinforcing cycle: by constantly scanning for threats, he began to see danger in harmless strangers, which in turn heightened his sense of an ever‑present menace. That increased threat feeling then pulled up more memory fragments—the smell of gunpowder, the wet sound of her breath stopping. The more he tried to push the memories away with overeating or avoidance, the more they seemed to intrude anyway, each fragment sharpened by the guilt and grief that were now inseparable from the event itself. He had lost count of how many evenings he spent pacing the house, checking the locks again, then sitting down to a meal he did not taste, all while the memory of her head turning toward him before the shot played on a loop in his mind.

Thong’s daughter finally convinced him to come for help after he spent an entire night with the kitchen light on, refusing to go upstairs because he thought he heard footsteps. He knows that his fear and his anger at the man who shot Lan are poisoning the years he has left, and he hopes—though he can barely say it—that talking might loosen the grip of those fragmented shards long enough for him to feel something other than vigilance and grief.
